posts.post_content: Who first described and named "Newcastle disease" after Newcastle-upon-Tyne, England?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Doyle (1927) described the disease in Newcastle-upon-Tyne and coined the name "Newcastle disease" as a temporary, non-descriptive term.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Edward (1927): Recorded the disease in India at Ranikhet the same year, giving rise to the name "Ranikhet disease", not the Newcastle name.
  • C. Java outbreak team (1926): The first outbreak was recorded in Java in 1926, before Doyle's description, but this earlier outbreak was not the source of the "Newcastle" name.
  • D. Metchnikoff (1884): Discovered phagocytosis, unrelated to Newcastle disease.

posts.post_content: Which NDV pathotype produces highly virulent disease with haemorrhagic intestinal lesions?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Viscerotropic velogenic NDV is highly virulent, producing haemorrhagic intestinal lesions.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Lentogenic: Causes only mild/inapparent respiratory infection, the opposite of a highly virulent haemorrhagic pathotype.
  • B. Mesogenic: Causes low mortality with respiratory ± nervous signs, less severe than viscerotropic velogenic disease.
  • D. Asymptomatic enteric: Causes inapparent enteric infection with no clinical signs, not haemorrhagic lesions.

posts.post_content: The confirmatory diagnostic test for Newcastle disease, based on a rise in paired-serum antibody titre, is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The Haemagglutination-inhibition (HI) test is the confirmation test; a rise in paired-serum HI antibody titre confirms infection.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Agar gel precipitin test: Listed as one of several "other serology" options, not the primary confirmation test for ND.
  • C. ELISA only: Also listed among other serology options, not singled out as the confirmation test.
  • D. Virus neutralisation in chick embryos: Another "other serology" option, not the primary HI-based confirmation method.

posts.post_content: NDV infection in humans (e.g. laboratory/vaccination staff) typically causes:

_aimcq_options.text: No infection is possible in humans

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

NDV can cause transitory human conjunctivitis, mainly in laboratory/vaccination staff and poultry-processing workers handling large virus quantities.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Fatal systemic illness: Not the reported human outcome; the effect is described as transitory and limited to conjunctivitis.
  • C. Chronic respiratory disease: Not the described human zoonotic effect of NDV.
  • D. No infection is possible in humans: Incorrect — NDV can cause human conjunctivitis in exposed workers.

posts.post_content: Infectious Bursal Disease virus primarily targets which cell type?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

IBDV primarily targets B-lymphocytes and their precursors in the bursa of Fabricius; T-lymphocytes are relatively spared.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. T-lymphocytes: Explicitly described as relatively spared by the virus, the opposite of the main target.
  • C. Neutrophils: Not the described target of IBDV; the virus is lymphotropic for B-cells.
  • D. Macrophages: Not the primary target described for IBDV pathogenesis.

posts.post_content: IBD virus is extremely stable in the environment, remaining infectious in the poultry house for up to:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

IBDV is extremely stable — infectious for up to 122 days in the poultry house, and beyond 52 days in water, feed and droppings.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. 7 days: Vastly underestimates the virus's environmental persistence.
  • B. 30 days: Still well short of the documented 122-day persistence in the house.
  • D. 365 days: Overstates the documented persistence figure of 122 days in the house.

posts.post_content: The bursa in IBD becomes atrophic by approximately which day post-infection?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The bursa is enlarged/oedematous early, becoming atrophic by day 3–8 — the hallmark lesion of IBD.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Day 1: Too early — this is before the bursa even shows the initial enlarged/oedematous phase.
  • C. Day 20: Well beyond the documented atrophy timeline of day 3–8.
  • D. Day 60: Far beyond the acute atrophy window described for IBD.

posts.post_content: Chemical bursectomy in IBD pathogenesis experiments is achieved using which agent?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Cyclophosphamide-induced chemical bursectomy in 3-day-old chicks confers resistance to later IBDV challenge, proving the bursa is the essential target organ.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Corticosteroids: Not the agent described for chemical bursectomy in this experimental model.
  • C. Aflatoxin: A mycotoxin causing immunosuppression via other mechanisms, not the bursectomy agent used here.
  • D. Amprolium: An anticoccidial/thiamine antagonist, unrelated to bursectomy.

posts.post_content: The "3 R's" of Infectious Bronchitis tissue tropism refer to:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The "3 R's" refer to Respiratory, Renal, and Reproductive tropism, reflecting the different serotype-associated tissue targets of IB virus.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Rapid, Recurrent, Resistant: Not the terminology used for IB tissue tropism.
  • C. Respiratory, Rectal, Renal: "Rectal" tropism is not a recognised IB category; reproductive tropism is the correct third R.
  • D. Reproductive, Retinal, Renal: "Retinal" tropism is not described; respiratory tropism is the correct first R.

posts.post_content: Which IB virus serotypes are nephrotoxic?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

T, Gray and Holte serotypes are nephrotoxic, while Massachusetts and Connecticut serotypes are respiratory.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Massachusetts and Connecticut: These are the respiratory serotypes, the opposite of nephrotoxic.
  • C. Only Massachusetts: Massachusetts is respiratory, not nephrotoxic, and the nephrotoxic group includes three named serotypes, not one.
  • D. All serotypes equally: Incorrect — different serotypes show distinct tissue tropism (the "3 R's"), not uniform nephrotoxicity.

posts.post_content: "Blind layer" syndrome in IB refers to:

_aimcq_options.text: Partial/complete oviduct failure from young-chick infection

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

"Blind layer" describes partial/complete oviduct failure resulting from IB infection of young chicks, leaving them unable to lay eggs normally as adults.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Corneal opacity from photosensitisation: Not an IB-related finding; this is unrelated to the blind layer phenomenon.
  • C. Kidney failure in growing birds: Describes the renal (nephritic) form of IB, a distinct presentation from blind layer.
  • D. Tracheal obstruction causing hypoxia: Relates to the respiratory form, not the reproductive tract damage described as blind layer.

posts.post_content: Among IB serological tests, which is described as the most sensitive?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

ELISA is described as the most sensitive serological test for IB, among virus neutralisation, immunodiffusion, HI and immunofluorescence.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Virus neutralisation: A valid IB serology method, but not the one singled out as most sensitive.
  • B. Immunodiffusion: Also a valid method, but not identified as the most sensitive test.
  • C. HI: Used for IB serology, but ELISA is specifically noted as the most sensitive.

posts.post_content: The diagnostic microscopic hallmark of ILT is:

_aimcq_options.text: Intranuclear inclusion bodies in tracheal epithelium

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Intranuclear inclusion bodies in tracheal epithelium are the diagnostic microscopic hallmark of ILT (a herpesvirus disease), seen early (day 1–5).

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions: Characteristic of fowl pox (Bollinger bodies), not ILT, which shows intranuclear inclusions.
  • C. Basophilic hepatocyte inclusions: Associated with inclusion body hepatitis (adenovirus), not ILT.
  • D. Bollinger bodies: The intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies of fowl pox, not the intranuclear inclusions of ILT.

posts.post_content: ILT virus can be grown on which structure of the embryonated egg?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

ILT virus can be grown on the chorioallantoic membrane (CAM) of embryonated eggs.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Allantoic sac: This is the site used for growing avian influenza virus, not the specific method described for ILT.
  • C. Amniotic cavity: Not the culture site described for ILT virus.
  • D. Yolk sac: Not the culture site described for ILT virus in this text.

posts.post_content: Which of the following predisposes birds to ILT?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Vitamin A deficiency and ammonia are cited as predisposing factors for ILT, along with concurrent infections (ND, IB, fowl pox, coryza, CRD).

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Excess vitamin D: Not listed as a predisposing factor for ILT.
  • C. Low ambient humidity only: Not the specific predisposing factor described; ammonia (not humidity) is named.
  • D. Excess dietary calcium: Not associated with ILT predisposition in this text.

posts.post_content: The peracute form of ILT is characterized by:

_aimcq_options.text: Death with no signs, or severe dyspnoea/coughing with bloody exudate
Asymptomatic infection unnoticed in the flock

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The peracute form shows death with no signs, or dyspnoea/severe coughing/expectoration of bloody exudate.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Mild moist rales only: Describes the mild form of ILT, not the peracute form.
  • C. Asymptomatic infection unnoticed in the flock: Describes the asymptomatic form, not peracute.
  • D. Chronic weight loss over months: Not a described feature of any ILT clinical form; ILT forms are peracute, acute, mild or asymptomatic, with acute death in 3-4 days or recovery in 2-3 weeks.

posts.post_content: Fowl pox virus is notable for being:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Fowl pox virus is the largest known avian virus (dsDNA, family Poxviridae), unusual in replicating within the cell cytoplasm.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. The smallest known avian virus: The opposite of the correct description — fowl pox is the largest, not smallest.
  • C. A single-stranded RNA virus: Incorrect — fowl pox virus is a double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) virus.
  • D. Unable to survive in scabs: Incorrect — infected cells sloughed into scabs remain infectious in the environment and are resistant to drying.

posts.post_content: Bollinger bodies in fowl pox contain which structures?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Bollinger bodies are intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies containing complete virions called Borrel granules.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Negri bodies: Associated with rabies, not fowl pox.
  • C. LCL bodies: Associated with avian chlamydiosis (Levinthal, Coles, Lillie bodies), not fowl pox.
  • D. Heat shock proteins: Cellular chaperone proteins, unrelated to fowl pox inclusion body content.

posts.post_content: Fowl pox virus requires which condition for successful entry and infection?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Fowl pox virus does not penetrate intact skin — a break in the skin is required for entry, replication and disease.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Intact, unbroken skin: This is exactly what the virus cannot penetrate — the opposite of the actual entry requirement.
  • C. Direct intravenous inoculation only: Not the natural entry route described; a skin break (from vaccination crews, biting insects, etc.) is the entry mechanism.
  • D. Prior vaccination against ILT: Unrelated to fowl pox entry mechanism.

posts.post_content: The diphtheritic (wet pox) form of fowl pox produces lesions primarily in which location?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The diphtheritic (wet pox) form produces fibrino-necrotic, proliferative lesions of the upper respiratory tract, mouth and oesophagus mucosa.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Unfeathered skin of head/neck/legs: This describes the cutaneous (dry pox) form, not the diphtheritic form.
  • C. Kidney and ureters: Not a site affected by fowl pox in either form.
  • D. Bursa of Fabricius: Not a fowl pox target; the bursa is the target organ in IBD, not fowl pox.

posts.post_content: Avian influenza viruses are subtyped based on how many haemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N) types?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

AI viruses are divided into 15 haemagglutinin (H1-15) and 9 neuraminidase (N1-9) subtypes by HI and NI tests respectively.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. 10 H and 5 N: Underestimates both the H and N subtype counts.
  • C. 5 H and 3 N: Substantially underestimates the actual subtype numbers.
  • D. 20 H and 15 N: Overestimates both subtype counts beyond the documented 15 H/9 N.

posts.post_content: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) strains typically arise from mutation of which subtypes?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

HP viruses arise by mutation of some H5 and H7 LP viruses, causing devastating epizootics.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. H1 and N1: Not the subtypes associated with HPAI emergence in poultry in this text.
  • C. H9 and N2: Not identified as the HPAI-capable subtypes here.
  • D. H3 and N8: Not the subtypes described as capable of HPAI mutation.

posts.post_content: A key laboratory clue distinguishing AI from Newcastle disease is that AI haemagglutination:

_aimcq_options.text: Is NOT inhibited by ND or other paramyxoviral antiserum
Cannot be demonstrated in the allantoic sac

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

AI haemagglutination is NOT inhibited by ND or other paramyxoviral antiserum — a key differential laboratory clue distinguishing AI from ND.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Is inhibited by ND antiserum: The opposite of the actual finding — AI haemagglutination is specifically NOT inhibited by ND antiserum.
  • C. Cannot be demonstrated in the allantoic sac: Incorrect — AI virus grows well in the allantoic sac of embryonating eggs and agglutinates RBCs there.
  • D. Requires mammalian RBCs only: Not stated; the haemagglutination property relates to its resistance to ND antiserum inhibition, not RBC species requirement.

posts.post_content: The 2004 H5N1 outbreak across Asian countries produced confirmed human cases in Thailand/Vietnam with a case-fatality rate of approximately:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The 2004 H5N1 outbreak produced 37 confirmed human cases in Thailand/Vietnam with a 68% case-fatality rate.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. 10%: Significantly underestimates the documented case-fatality rate.
  • B. 25%: Still well below the documented 68% figure.
  • C. 50%: Closer but still below the documented 68% case-fatality rate.

posts.post_content: Which Marek's disease serotype is the avirulent turkey herpesvirus used as a vaccine?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Serotype 3, the avirulent turkey herpesvirus (HVT), is used as a vaccine.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Serotype 1: The virulent chicken isolate serotype, causing disease, not the vaccine strain.
  • B. Serotype 2: An avirulent chicken isolate also used as vaccine, but the turkey herpesvirus (HVT) specifically is serotype 3.
  • D. Serotype 4: Not a recognised Marek's disease serotype; only three serotypes are described.

posts.post_content: The classic clinical posture in Marek's disease is:

_aimcq_options.text: Unilateral leg paresis — one leg forward, one backward
Wing drop with both legs paralysed equally

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The classic posture is transient unilateral leg paresis — one leg forward, one backward.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Torticollis with opisthotonus: More characteristic of conditions like avian encephalomyelitis or vitamin E deficiency (encephalomalacia), not the classic MD posture.
  • C. Wing drop with both legs paralysed equally: MD classically shows unilateral, not symmetric bilateral, leg involvement.
  • D. Head tremor with ataxia: More characteristic of avian encephalomyelitis, not the classic MD leg posture.

posts.post_content: A key differential feature distinguishing Marek's disease from lymphoid leukosis is:

_aimcq_options.text: MD bursa is rarely tumorous (usually atrophic); leukosis bursa is near-pathognomonically tumorous
MD only affects turkeys; leukosis only affects chickens
MD is egg-transmitted; leukosis is not
MD causes no nerve enlargement; leukosis always does

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The bursa is rarely tumorous in MD (more often atrophic), whereas bursal involvement is near-pathognomonic in lymphoid leukosis — a key differential point.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. MD only affects turkeys; leukosis only affects chickens: Incorrect — chickens are the most important natural host for MD; leukosis viruses also cause disease specifically in chickens, not turkeys exclusively.
  • C. MD is egg-transmitted; leukosis is not: The reverse is true — MD is explicitly NOT vertically transmitted, while avian leukosis virus IS shed into the egg (vertical transmission).
  • D. MD causes no nerve enlargement; leukosis always does: Incorrect — MD classically causes enlarged, non-striated peripheral nerves; nerve enlargement is not the leukosis hallmark.

posts.post_content: Marek's disease can appear as early as what age, compared to lymphoid leukosis (typically after 14 weeks)?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

MD can appear as early as 3 weeks of age, compared with lymphoid leukosis, which typically appears after 14 weeks.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. 8 weeks: Later than the documented earliest onset of 3 weeks for MD.
  • C. 20 weeks: Well beyond the earliest documented MD onset age.
  • D. 1 year: Far beyond the described early-onset window for MD.

posts.post_content: Avian leukosis virus subgroup J is specifically associated with:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Subgroup J is associated with myeloid neoplasms/myelocytoma in broiler-breeders, first isolated in England.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Lymphoid leukosis (Big Liver Disease): Historically associated with subgroups A and B, not specifically subgroup J.
  • C. Endogenous, rarely oncogenic infection: Describes subgroup E, not subgroup J.
  • D. Renal tumours only: Not the specific association described for subgroup J.

posts.post_content: Lymphoid leukosis is a clonal malignancy of which cell lineage?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Lymphoid leukosis is a clonal B-lymphocyte malignancy of the bursal-dependent lymphoid system, with transformation occurring in the intact bursa.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. T-lymphocytes: T-cell lymphomas are characteristic of Marek's disease/reticuloendotheliosis, not lymphoid leukosis.
  • C. Myeloid precursors: This describes myeloid leukosis, a distinct malignancy from lymphoid leukosis.
  • D. Erythroid precursors: Not the cell lineage involved in lymphoid leukosis.

posts.post_content: Avian leukosis is distinguished from Marek's disease by demonstrating:

_aimcq_options.text: Clonal proviral DNA integration disrupting the c-myc oncogene

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Avian leukosis is distinguished from MD by demonstrating clonal proviral DNA integration disrupting the c-myc oncogene.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Enlarged peripheral nerves: A classic MD feature, not a leukosis-specific differentiating finding.
  • C. Grey eye (iris lymphoid infiltration): A classic MD finding (lymphoid infiltration of the iris), not the leukosis differentiator.
  • D. Feather follicle skin leukosis: A classic MD finding (enlarged feather follicles), not the molecular differentiator used for leukosis.

posts.post_content: The best control method for avian leukosis in primary breeder flocks is:

_aimcq_options.text: Testing egg albumen for viral antigen and discarding eggs from shedder hens
Culling all birds over 14 weeks of age

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Best control relies on testing egg albumen for viral antigen shedding and discarding eggs from shedder hens, since vaccination has not proven promising for tumour prevention.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Universal vaccination of all breeders: Vaccination has NOT proven promising for tumour prevention against avian leukosis, unlike other poultry viral diseases.
  • C. Antibiotic treatment of infected flocks: Antibiotics are ineffective against viral infections like avian leukosis.
  • D. Culling all birds over 14 weeks of age: Not the described control strategy; the focus is on albumen antigen testing of breeder hens, not age-based culling.

posts.post_content: Age resistance to avian encephalomyelitis is shown by bursectomy experiments to be:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Bursectomy (not thymectomy) abolishes age resistance, showing it is humoral-immunity based (bursa-dependent).

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Thymus-dependent (cell-mediated): Explicitly ruled out — thymectomy does NOT abolish age resistance, only bursectomy does.
  • C. Independent of the immune system: Incorrect — the bursectomy experiment specifically demonstrates immune (humoral) dependence.
  • D. Dependent on complement alone: Not the mechanism described; the evidence points to humoral (antibody-based) immunity via the bursa.

posts.post_content: Which finding is considered pathognomonic for avian encephalomyelitis?

_aimcq_options.text: Microgliosis of nucleus rotundus/ovoidalis and central chromatolysis

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Microgliosis in the nucleus rotundus and nucleus ovoidalis, plus central chromatolysis of brainstem/medullary neurons, are considered pathognomonic for AE.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Cerebellar oedema and haemorrhage: This is the pathognomonic finding for vitamin E deficiency (encephalomalacia), not AE.
  • C. Bursal atrophy by day 3-8: The hallmark lesion of IBD, not AE.
  • D. Enlarged non-striated peripheral nerves: The classic finding in Marek's disease, not AE.

posts.post_content: Survivors of avian encephalomyelitis may later develop which sequela?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Survivors may later develop lens opacity (bluish discolouration) causing blindness.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Permanent leg paralysis: Not the described AE survivor sequela; ataxia and tremor occur in the acute disease, but the classic survivor sequela is lens opacity.
  • C. Chronic renal failure: Not associated with AE; this is more characteristic of nephrotoxic IB or ochratoxicosis.
  • D. Feather follicle tumours: Associated with Marek's disease (skin leukosis), not AE.

posts.post_content: Vertical (egg) transmission of AE virus occurs during which window?

_aimcq_options.text: Only in the first week of a hen's life
3-4 weeks between hen infection and development of immunity
Only after the hen has fully recovered

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Vertical transmission occurs through the egg during the 3-4 week window between hen infection and development of immunity.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Only in the first week of a hen's life: Not the described window; it is tied to the period after infection, before immunity develops, not a fixed early-life window.
  • C. Only after the hen has fully recovered: Incorrect — transmission occurs during the window before immunity develops, not after recovery.
  • D. Never — AE is not egg-transmitted: Incorrect — vertical transmission is described as "very important" for AE.

posts.post_content: Inclusion Body Hepatitis is caused by which agent?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

IBH is caused by fowl Aviadenovirus group I; no separate "IBH virus" exists.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Circovirus: The agent responsible for chicken infectious anaemia, not IBH.
  • C. Birnavirus: The agent responsible for infectious bursal disease, not IBH.
  • D. Reovirus: The agent responsible for viral arthritis, not IBH.

posts.post_content: Hydropericardium syndrome (Litchi disease) is caused by:

_aimcq_options.text: An incomplete (defective) virus requiring a helper adenovirus
A circovirus requiring no helper virus

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Hydropericardium syndrome is caused by an incomplete (defective) virus requiring a helper adenovirus for replication.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. A complete, independently replicating adenovirus: Incorrect — the causative agent is specifically described as incomplete/defective, needing a helper virus.
  • C. A circovirus requiring no helper virus: Not the described agent; hydropericardium's causative agent is an adenovirus-related defective virus.
  • D. Bacterial toxin alone: Incorrect — the disease is viral in origin (defective adenovirus with implicated co-factors like aflatoxicosis).

posts.post_content: The diagnostic lesion for naturally occurring IBH cases is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Natural IBH cases mostly give eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions in hepatocytes on H&E staining, which is diagnostic.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Basophilic hepatocyte inclusions predominantly: This pattern is mostly seen with experimental infection, not the typical natural case pattern (which is eosinophilic).
  • C. Bollinger bodies: A fowl pox finding, not IBH.
  • D. Reed-Sternberg-like cells: Not a poultry pathology finding; irrelevant to IBH.

posts.post_content: Hydropericardium syndrome is called "Litchi disease" because of the resemblance of the:

_aimcq_options.text: Distended pericardial sac to a litchi fruit

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The distended pericardial sac, filled with straw-coloured fluid, resembles a litchi fruit, giving the disease its name.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Liver to a litchi fruit: The liver is described as swollen/discoloured, but the litchi comparison specifically applies to the distended pericardial sac.
  • C. Kidney lesions to litchi seeds: Kidneys are described as swollen with distended ureters, not compared to litchi seeds.
  • D. Feather pattern to litchi leaves: Not a described feature of hydropericardium syndrome.

posts.post_content: Chicken Infectious Anaemia Virus (CIAV) is classified under family:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

CIAV is a non-enveloped, single-stranded circular DNA virus classified under Circoviridae.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Adenoviridae: The family for IBH and EDS-76 causative agents, not CIA.
  • C. Birnaviridae: The family for the IBD virus, not CIA.
  • D. Herpesviridae: The family for ILT and Marek's disease viruses, not CIA.

posts.post_content: CIAV principally replicates in which cells?

_aimcq_options.text: Precursor T cells of the thymic cortex and bone-marrow haemocytoblasts

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

CIAV principally replicates in precursor T cells of the thymic cortex and haemocytoblasts of the bone marrow, whose destruction underlies the immunosuppression and anaemia.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. B-lymphocytes of the bursa: This is the target of IBDV, not CIAV.
  • C. Kupffer cells of the liver: Not the principal replication site described for CIAV.
  • D. Purkinje cells of the cerebellum: The favoured replication site of AE virus, not CIAV.

posts.post_content: The most characteristic gross lesion of chicken infectious anaemia is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Bone-marrow atrophy (fatty, yellowish-pink femoral marrow) is the most characteristic lesion; thymic atrophy is the most consistent lesion.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Bursal atrophy: Explicitly described as "less noticeable" in CIA — not the most characteristic finding.
  • C. Cerebellar haemorrhage: A vitamin E deficiency finding, not a CIA lesion.
  • D. Pericardial fluid accumulation: The hydropericardium syndrome finding, not CIA.

posts.post_content: Co-infection with which agents enhances CIAV pathogenicity and overcomes maternal antibody protection?

_aimcq_options.text: Reticuloendotheliosis virus, virulent MDV, or IBDV

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Dual infection with reticuloendotheliosis virus, virulent MDV, or IBDV enhances CAV pathogenicity and can overcome maternal-antibody protection.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Aspergillus fumigatus only: A fungal pathogen causing aspergillosis, not described as a CIA pathogenicity enhancer.
  • C. Salmonella pullorum only: Causes pullorum disease; not identified as a CIA co-infection enhancer.
  • D. E. coli O78 only: A colibacillosis-associated serotype, not a described CIA enhancer.

posts.post_content: Egg Drop Syndrome-76 is caused by:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

EDS-76 is caused by duck adenovirus A (Atadenovirus), serotype DAdV-1, naturally a waterfowl adenovirus that has infected domestic fowl.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Fowl Aviadenovirus group I: The IBH-causing agent, distinct from EDS-76's atadenovirus.
  • C. A birnavirus: The IBD-causing virus family, not EDS-76.
  • D. A coronavirus: The IB-causing virus family, not EDS-76.

posts.post_content: The three outbreak patterns of EDS-76 are:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

_aimcq_options.text: Is the essential carrier of Histomonas meleagridis

posts.post_content: The pathognomonic gross lesion of histomoniasis (blackhead) is:

Pericardial effusion resembling a litchi fruit

posts.post_content: The classic gross lesion of vitamin A deficiency in the oesophagus/crop/pharynx mucosa is:

_aimcq_options.text: White pustule-like nodules from squamous metaplasia of mucous glands

Vitamin A deficiency causes squamous metaplasia of mucous glands, producing characteristic small, white, pustule-like nodules in the oesophagus, pharynx and crop mucosa.

  • B. Diphtheritic pseudomembrane: A fowl pox (wet pox) finding, not the classic vitamin A deficiency lesion.
  • C. Caseous granulomas: An avian tuberculosis finding, not a vitamin A deficiency lesion.
  • D. Petechial haemorrhages: More associated with vitamin K deficiency or septicaemic disease, not the classic metaplastic vitamin A lesion.

posts.post_content: Vitamin A deficiency predisposes to which renal/urinary finding?

_aimcq_options.text: Urolithiasis with urate deposits in ureters/kidney
Chronic interstitial nephritis with contracted kidney

Squamous metaplasia of the ureteral/renal tubular epithelium leads to urate deposition and urolithiasis in the ureters and kidneys.

  • B. Chronic interstitial nephritis with contracted kidney: Not the specific vitamin A deficiency mechanism, which relates to metaplasia and urate obstruction, not chronic interstitial inflammation.
  • C. Amyloidosis: Not associated with vitamin A deficiency; amyloid deposition has a distinct immune-related pathogenesis.

posts.post_content: Severe vitamin A deficiency in growing chicks causes which ocular sign?

_aimcq_options.text: Xerophthalmia with caseous exudate under the eyelids

Severe deficiency causes xerophthalmia (dryness) with accumulation of caseous exudate under the eyelids, sometimes leading to blindness.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Cataract with blue lens opacity: A classic avian encephalomyelitis survivor sequela, not a vitamin A deficiency sign.
  • C. Panophthalmitis from bacterial infection only: Not the primary described mechanism; the deficiency itself directly causes epithelial keratinisation and xerophthalmia.
  • D. Retinal detachment: Not a described feature of vitamin A deficiency in poultry.

posts.post_content: Vitamin A deficiency is prevented mainly by dietary supplementation with:

_aimcq_options.text: Preformed vitamin A or its precursor carotene

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Deficiency is prevented by adequate dietary preformed vitamin A or its precursor carotene (found in green feeds/yellow corn); requirements increase with high production/disease stress.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Vitamin D3 alone: Addresses calcium/phosphorus metabolism (rickets), not vitamin A deficiency.
  • C. Selenium and vitamin E combined: Addresses a separate deficiency syndrome (encephalomalacia/exudative diathesis), not vitamin A deficiency.
  • D. Excess dietary protein: Not the corrective nutrient for vitamin A deficiency.

posts.post_content: Vitamin D deficiency produces rickets primarily because it impairs:

_aimcq_options.text: Intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphorus

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Vitamin D is essential for intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphorus; deficiency impairs bone mineralisation, producing rickets in young birds.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Collagen crosslinking in tendons: Not the vitamin D mechanism; this relates more to connective tissue/copper metabolism issues, not rickets pathogenesis.
  • C. Iron absorption for haemoglobin synthesis: Unrelated to vitamin D's role; iron absorption relates to anaemia, not rickets.
  • D. Vitamin K-dependent clotting factor synthesis: The mechanism of vitamin K, not vitamin D.

posts.post_content: Rickets in young growing chicks characteristically causes:

_aimcq_options.text: Soft, pliable, easily bent long bones and beak
Hard, brittle bones with pathological fractures only in adults

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Rickets in young chicks produces soft, pliable bones and beak that bend easily, with enlarged costochondral junctions (rachitic rosary) and leg deformities.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Hard, brittle bones with pathological fractures only in adults: The opposite finding — bones become soft/pliable in young rickets, not hard/brittle; the adult counterpart (osteomalacia) shows softening too, not brittleness.
  • C. Cerebellar hypoplasia: Not a described feature of vitamin D deficiency; this is unrelated to bone mineralisation.
  • D. Feather loss without skeletal change: Rickets is fundamentally a skeletal disease; feather loss is not its characteristic sign.

posts.post_content: Vitamin D deficiency in laying hens produces which egg-related finding?

_aimcq_options.text: Thin-shelled or shell-less eggs with reduced hatchability

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

In layers, deficiency causes thin-shelled or shell-less eggs and reduced hatchability, along with decreased egg production, reflecting impaired calcium mobilisation for shell formation.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Double-yolked eggs: A reproductive/ovulation timing phenomenon, not a described vitamin D deficiency effect.
  • C. Eggs with excessive pigment: Not related to vitamin D status; pigment relates to porphyrin deposition in the shell gland.
  • D. No effect on egg production: Incorrect — vitamin D deficiency significantly reduces egg production and shell quality.

posts.post_content: Osteomalacia, as opposed to rickets, occurs in which age group?

_aimcq_options.text: Adult/mature birds with previously normal bone

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Osteomalacia refers to demineralisation of previously normal bone in adult/mature birds, distinct from rickets, which affects the growing skeleton of young birds.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Only in day-old chicks: This age group is associated with rickets, not osteomalacia, which specifically affects mature bone.
  • C. Only in embryos: Not the age group associated with osteomalacia.
  • D. Only in males: Sex is not the distinguishing factor between rickets and osteomalacia; age/bone maturity is.

posts.post_content: Encephalomalacia (crazy chick disease) from vitamin E deficiency is characterized by:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Encephalomalacia is characterized by cerebellar oedema, haemorrhage and softening (malacia), producing ataxia, tremor and opisthotonus in young chicks.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Bursal atrophy: An IBD-related finding, not a vitamin E deficiency lesion.
  • C. Copper-bronze liver: The acute fowl typhoid finding, not vitamin E deficiency.
  • D. Renal urate deposits: A gout-related finding, not the vitamin E deficiency encephalomalacia lesion.

posts.post_content: Exudative diathesis, a vitamin E/selenium deficiency syndrome, is characterized by:

_aimcq_options.text: Subcutaneous oedema from increased capillary permeability

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Exudative diathesis results from increased capillary permeability, producing greenish-blue subcutaneous oedema (fluid accumulation), typically over the breast and ventral body.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Dry, flaky skin with hyperkeratosis: The opposite mechanism — exudative diathesis involves fluid accumulation/oedema, not dryness/keratinisation.
  • C. Cerebellar tumours: Not associated with exudative diathesis; this syndrome is a vascular permeability disorder, not neoplastic.
  • D. Chronic pancreatitis: Not the described mechanism or lesion of exudative diathesis.

posts.post_content: Nutritional muscular dystrophy from vitamin E/selenium deficiency shows which gross finding in skeletal muscle?

_aimcq_options.text: Pale streaks of degeneration ("white muscle disease")

Correct Answer Explanation

Muscular dystrophy shows pale streaks of muscle degeneration, giving the classic appearance of "white muscle disease", primarily in the breast and leg muscles.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Melanotic pigmentation: Not a feature of nutritional muscular dystrophy.
  • C. Caseous granulomas: An infectious/tuberculous finding, not a nutritional myopathy feature.
  • D. Gas bubbles with crepitation: A gangrenous dermatitis (clostridial) finding, not nutritional muscular dystrophy.

posts.post_content: Vitamin E and selenium deficiency syndromes overlap because both nutrients function together as:

_aimcq_options.text: Antioxidants protecting cell membranes from lipid peroxidation

Correct Answer Explanation

Vitamin E and selenium (as part of glutathione peroxidase) both function as antioxidants protecting cell membranes from lipid peroxidation, explaining their overlapping deficiency syndromes.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Cofactors for calcium absorption: This is the role of vitamin D, not vitamin E/selenium.
  • C. Components of haemoglobin synthesis: Not the shared function of vitamin E and selenium.
  • D. Precursors of vitamin K: Vitamin E and K are distinct fat-soluble vitamins with separate functions, not precursor-product related.

posts.post_content: Vitamin K deficiency causes a bleeding tendency because it is required for:

_aimcq_options.text: Hepatic synthesis of prothrombin and other clotting factors

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Vitamin K is required for hepatic synthesis of prothrombin and other clotting factors; deficiency causes prolonged clotting time and haemorrhagic tendency.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Platelet production in bone marrow: Not vitamin K's role; thrombocytopenia is a distinct mechanism from clotting factor synthesis.
  • C. Vascular endothelial integrity directly: This is more related to vitamin C's role, not vitamin K's clotting-factor function.
  • D. Fibrinolysis: Vitamin K supports clot formation, not the breakdown (fibrinolysis) of clots.

posts.post_content: Subclinical vitamin K deficiency in poultry commonly results from:

_aimcq_options.text: Sulfa drug administration or mycotoxin-damaged intestine

Correct Answer Explanation

Deficiency commonly results from sulfa drug administration (which inhibits intestinal bacterial vitamin K synthesis) or a mycotoxin-damaged intestine impairing absorption.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Excess dietary calcium: Not a described cause of vitamin K deficiency; calcium excess relates more to renal/gout issues.
  • C. Excess dietary vitamin A: Not a described cause of vitamin K deficiency.
  • D. Cold stress alone: Not identified as a cause of vitamin K deficiency in this context.

posts.post_content: Birds with vitamin K deficiency characteristically show:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Deficient birds show extensive subcutaneous and intramuscular haemorrhages, often triggered by minor trauma, along with prolonged clotting time.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Rachitic rosary of the ribs: A vitamin D deficiency (rickets) finding, not vitamin K deficiency.
  • C. White pustules in the crop: A vitamin A deficiency finding, not vitamin K deficiency.
  • D. Cerebellar softening: A vitamin E deficiency (encephalomalacia) finding, not vitamin K deficiency.

posts.post_content: Which class of compounds acts as vitamin K antagonists, capable of inducing deficiency?

Coumarin-type anticoagulants, such as dicoumarol from spoiled sweet clover or certain rodenticides, act as vitamin K antagonists and can induce deficiency-like haemorrhagic disease.

  • C. Aminoglycosides: Not a vitamin K antagonist class.
  • D. Beta-lactam antibiotics: Not associated with vitamin K antagonism in this context.

posts.post_content: The classic clinical sign of thiamine (B1) deficiency in chicks is:

posts.post_content: The classic clinical sign of riboflavin (B2) deficiency in chicks is:

_aimcq_options.text: Curled toe paralysis with birds walking on hocks

Riboflavin deficiency causes curled toe paralysis from peripheral nerve degeneration, with affected chicks walking on their hocks with curled toes.

posts.post_content: Riboflavin deficiency causes which characteristic nerve change, visible grossly?

Complete nerve atrophy with no enlargement

Riboflavin deficiency causes enlarged, soft, oedematous sciatic and brachial nerves due to demyelination and Schwann cell proliferation.

  • B. Complete nerve atrophy with no enlargement: The opposite of the actual finding — nerves become enlarged/oedematous, not atrophic.
  • C. Nerve calcification: Not the described riboflavin deficiency nerve lesion.
  • D. Nerve pigmentation: Not a described feature of riboflavin deficiency.

posts.post_content: Riboflavin deficiency in breeder hens leads to which hatching defect in embryos?

posts.post_content: Pantothenic acid deficiency in chicks classically causes:

posts.post_content: Niacin deficiency in poultry (especially turkeys) causes:

  • B. Curled toe paralysis: The classic riboflavin deficiency sign, not niacin deficiency.

posts.post_content: Pyridoxine (B6) deficiency in chicks is characterized by:

posts.post_content: Most B-complex vitamin deficiencies in growing chicks share which common general feature?

posts.post_content: Fatty Liver and Kidney Syndrome (FLKS) in chicks is primarily linked to deficiency of:

posts.post_content: Reduced biotin bioavailability in certain feed ingredients (e.g. wheat, barley) can predispose to deficiency because:

posts.post_content: Folic acid deficiency in growing chicks characteristically causes:

posts.post_content: Choline deficiency in young chicks causes:

posts.post_content: Vitamin B12 deficiency in poultry primarily causes:

_aimcq_options.text: Poor growth, poor feathering, and reduced hatchability

Vitamin B12 deficiency causes poor growth, poor feathering, and reduced hatchability in breeder flocks, as it is essential for nucleic acid/protein synthesis.

posts.post_content: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency is uncommon in poultry primarily because:

Vitamin C is not required by birds at all

posts.post_content: Calcium deficiency in laying hens characteristically causes:

  • B. Perosis: Associated with manganese/choline/biotin deficiency, not primarily calcium deficiency.

posts.post_content: Proper bone mineralisation depends not just on absolute calcium/phosphorus levels but also on:

_aimcq_options.text: An appropriate calcium:phosphorus ratio plus adequate vitamin D

Proper mineralisation requires an appropriate calcium:phosphorus ratio together with adequate vitamin D, since imbalance (even with adequate absolute amounts) can impair absorption/utilisation.

  • B. High dietary protein alone: Not the key factor for mineralisation described here; the Ca:P ratio and vitamin D are.

posts.post_content: Excess dietary phosphorus relative to calcium can lead to:

_aimcq_options.text: Secondary nutritional hyperparathyroidism with bone resorption
No adverse effect regardless of calcium level

Excess phosphorus relative to calcium can cause secondary nutritional hyperparathyroidism, with resultant bone resorption as the body attempts to correct the imbalance.

  • B. No adverse effect regardless of calcium level: Incorrect — the Ca:P ratio matters significantly for skeletal health, not just absolute phosphorus levels.

posts.post_content: Calcium (and/or vitamin D) deficiency in growing (non-laying) chicks primarily manifests as:

In growing chicks, calcium/vitamin D deficiency primarily manifests as rickets with bone deformity, since there is no laying-related calcium demand yet — the skeletal growth process itself is impaired.

posts.post_content: Sodium/chloride deficiency in growing chicks causes:

Sodium/chloride deficiency causes poor growth, increased cannibalism/feather-picking tendencies, and adrenal hypertrophy, reflecting the electrolyte's role in growth and behaviour regulation.

  • B. Rachitic rosary: A vitamin D deficiency sign, not sodium/chloride deficiency.

posts.post_content: Salt (sodium chloride) poisoning in poultry is most dangerous when combined with:

posts.post_content: Salt poisoning in poultry produces which gross finding?

Salt poisoning causes subcutaneous and visceral oedema/ascites from disturbed fluid balance secondary to the sodium overload.

  • B. Bursal atrophy: An IBD-related finding, not salt poisoning.
  • C. Copper-bronze liver: The acute fowl typhoid finding, not salt poisoning.
  • D. Caseous middle-ear exudate: A chronic fowl cholera finding, not salt poisoning.

posts.post_content: The link between sodium/chloride deficiency and cannibalism/feather picking suggests that management of vices should include checking:

Because sodium/chloride deficiency is a recognised contributor to cannibalism and feather-picking tendencies, checking dietary salt adequacy is an important part of investigating/managing these vices.

  • D. Only beak length: Related to management (trimming), not the underlying nutritional deficiency link being asked about.

posts.post_content: The classic sign of manganese deficiency in growing chicks is:

Correct Answer Explanation

Manganese deficiency causes perosis (slipped Achilles tendon) with twisted, bowed leg bones, due to impaired cartilage matrix (mucopolysaccharide) synthesis.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Curled toe paralysis: The classic riboflavin deficiency sign, not manganese deficiency.
  • C. Xerophthalmia: A vitamin A deficiency sign, not manganese deficiency.
  • D. Rachitic rosary: A vitamin D deficiency sign, not manganese deficiency.

posts.post_content: Manganese deficiency in breeder hens causes which embryonic defect?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Deficiency in breeders causes embryonic chondrodystrophy, producing short/thickened legs and wings, and a characteristic "parrot beak" appearance, with reduced hatchability.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Anaemia only: Not the classic manganese deficiency embryo defect; the skeletal chondrodystrophy is specifically described.
  • C. Cataracts only: Not the classic manganese deficiency finding; cataracts are more associated with AE survivor sequelae.
  • D. No effect on the embryo: Incorrect — manganese deficiency significantly affects embryonic skeletal development and hatchability.

posts.post_content: Manganese's role in preventing perosis relates to its function as a cofactor for:

_aimcq_options.text: Enzymes involved in mucopolysaccharide (cartilage matrix) synthesis

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Manganese acts as a cofactor for enzymes involved in mucopolysaccharide (cartilage matrix) synthesis, essential for normal cartilage/tendon development, explaining the perosis link.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Haemoglobin synthesis: Primarily an iron-dependent process, not the manganese mechanism described for perosis.
  • C. Vitamin K activation: Not the manganese mechanism relevant to skeletal/tendon development.
  • D. Fat digestion: Not the described role of manganese in preventing perosis.

posts.post_content: High dietary calcium levels can worsen manganese deficiency because they:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

High dietary calcium can reduce manganese absorption/availability, worsening the risk of manganese deficiency even when total dietary manganese appears adequate.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Increase manganese absorption excessively: The opposite of the actual interaction — high calcium reduces, not increases, manganese availability.
  • C. Have no interaction with manganese: Incorrect — a well-recognised antagonistic interaction exists between calcium and manganese availability.
  • D. Directly destroy dietary manganese: Not the described mechanism; the interaction is about reduced absorption, not chemical destruction.

posts.post_content: Zinc deficiency in growing chicks characteristically causes:

_aimcq_options.text: Poor feathering, short/thickened long bones, and enlarged hocks

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Zinc deficiency causes poor feathering, short/thickened long bones, and enlarged hock joints, since zinc is a cofactor for many enzymes involved in growth and keratin formation.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Curled toe paralysis: The classic riboflavin deficiency sign, not zinc deficiency.
  • C. Xerophthalmia: A vitamin A deficiency sign, not zinc deficiency.
  • D. Cerebellar softening: A vitamin E deficiency sign, not zinc deficiency.

posts.post_content: Zinc deficiency also causes which skin-related finding?

_aimcq_options.text: Dermatitis, particularly around the feet, hocks and vent

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Zinc deficiency causes dermatitis, particularly around the feet, hocks and vent, reflecting zinc's role in epithelial integrity and keratinisation.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Exudative diathesis: A vitamin E/selenium deficiency sign, not zinc deficiency.
  • C. Xerophthalmia of the eyelids: A vitamin A deficiency sign, not zinc deficiency.
  • D. Fowl pox-like lesions: A viral (poxvirus) disease finding, distinct from the nutritional dermatitis of zinc deficiency.

posts.post_content: Excess dietary calcium can worsen zinc deficiency because it:

_aimcq_options.text: Increases zinc excretion via bile only
Has no known interaction with zinc
Converts zinc to a toxic form

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Excess dietary calcium can interfere with zinc absorption, similar to its antagonistic effect on manganese, worsening the risk of zinc deficiency.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Increases zinc excretion via bile only: Not the specifically described mechanism; the interaction is about reduced absorption, not enhanced biliary excretion.
  • C. Has no known interaction with zinc: Incorrect — a recognised calcium-zinc antagonism affecting absorption exists.
  • D. Converts zinc to a toxic form: Not the described mechanism of the calcium-zinc interaction.

posts.post_content: Zinc deficiency in breeder hens is associated with:

_aimcq_options.text: Reduced hatchability and skeletal deformities in embryos

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Zinc deficiency in breeders is associated with reduced hatchability and skeletal deformities in embryos, given zinc's essential role in numerous metalloenzymes required for normal development.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Improved eggshell quality: The opposite of the actual effect — deficiency impairs, rather than improves, reproductive outcomes.
  • C. No reproductive effects: Incorrect — zinc deficiency has clear negative reproductive/hatchability effects.
  • D. Increased egg size only: Not a described effect of zinc deficiency; the key effects are on hatchability and embryo skeletal development.

posts.post_content: Selenium deficiency in poultry overlaps clinically with which vitamin's deficiency syndrome?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Selenium deficiency overlaps with vitamin E deficiency, since selenium is a component of glutathione peroxidase, working alongside vitamin E as part of the antioxidant defence system.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Vitamin A: Not the overlapping deficiency syndrome for selenium; vitamin A deficiency has a distinct epithelial/xerophthalmic presentation.
  • C. Vitamin D: Not the overlapping deficiency syndrome; vitamin D deficiency relates to calcium/phosphorus metabolism, not the selenium-vitamin E antioxidant axis.
  • D. Vitamin K: Not the overlapping deficiency syndrome; vitamin K deficiency causes haemorrhagic disease, unrelated to selenium's antioxidant role.

posts.post_content: Selenium deficiency contributes to which specific muscle condition, alongside vitamin E deficiency?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Selenium deficiency, together with vitamin E deficiency, contributes to nutritional muscular dystrophy ("white muscle disease"), characterized by pale degenerative streaks in skeletal muscle.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Gas gangrene: An infectious clostridial condition, unrelated to selenium deficiency.
  • C. Tenosynovitis: Associated with M. synoviae or reovirus infection, not selenium deficiency.
  • D. Muscular hypertrophy: The opposite finding — selenium deficiency causes muscle degeneration (dystrophy), not hypertrophy.

posts.post_content: Unlike deficiency, selenium toxicity/excess in poultry can cause:

_aimcq_options.text: Reduced hatchability and embryo deformities from excess dietary selenium
No adverse effects at high doses

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Selenium has a narrow margin of safety — excess dietary selenium can also cause reduced hatchability and embryo deformities, distinct from but paralleling the reproductive effects of deficiency.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Muscular dystrophy identical to deficiency: Toxicity and deficiency produce distinct effects, not identical presentations; toxicity is not simply "more of the deficiency picture".
  • C. No adverse effects at high doses: Incorrect — selenium's narrow margin of safety means excess is harmful, not innocuous.
  • D. Improved growth at all doses: Incorrect — selenium requirements follow a narrow optimal range, not a dose where "more is always better".

posts.post_content: Fatty Liver-Haemorrhagic Syndrome (FLHS) typically affects which type of bird?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

FLHS typically affects overweight, high-producing caged laying hens, related to excessive energy intake and hepatic fat accumulation.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Underweight range-reared pullets: The opposite bird profile — FLHS is specifically linked to overweight, high-producing hens, not underweight birds.
  • C. Day-old broiler chicks: FLHS is a laying-hen condition tied to sustained high egg production and excess energy intake, not a day-old chick condition.
  • D. Breeding toms (male turkeys): Not the typical bird type for FLHS, which is specifically described in laying hens.

posts.post_content: FLHS results from excessive hepatic fat accumulation combined with:

_aimcq_options.text: Rupture of fragile, fat-infiltrated liver causing fatal haemorrhage

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The fat-laden liver becomes fragile, and minor trauma (e.g. during oviposition straining) can cause rupture and fatal internal haemorrhage.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Bacterial liver abscessation: Not the described mechanism of FLHS; the pathogenesis is metabolic (fat infiltration) plus mechanical rupture, not infection.
  • C. Viral hepatocyte necrosis: Not the FLHS mechanism, which is a nutritional/metabolic disorder, not an infectious one.
  • D. Amyloid deposition in the liver: Not part of FLHS pathogenesis; amyloidosis is a distinct immune-related process.

posts.post_content: Prevention of FLHS in layer flocks primarily involves:

_aimcq_options.text: Controlling caloric/energy intake to prevent excess bird weight

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Prevention primarily involves controlling caloric/energy intake to prevent excess bird weight, since obesity and excess energy intake are the key predisposing factors.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Increasing dietary fat further: Would worsen, not prevent, the hepatic fat accumulation underlying FLHS.
  • C. Eliminating all dietary carbohydrate: Not the described preventive approach; the key is overall energy control, not eliminating one macronutrient entirely.
  • D. Increasing stocking density: Not related to FLHS prevention; this is more relevant to behavioural vices like cannibalism.

posts.post_content: Which of the following is a recognised predisposing factor for cannibalism in poultry flocks?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Overcrowding and excessive light intensity are recognised predisposing factors, along with nutritional deficiencies (e.g. sodium/protein), boredom, and injury exposing blood.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Adequate perch space: A protective/preventive factor, not a predisposing cause of cannibalism.
  • C. Low stocking density: Reduces, rather than predisposes to, cannibalism — overcrowding (high density) is the actual risk factor.
  • D. Dim, low-intensity lighting: This is actually protective/preventive, as reduced light intensity is a common management strategy used to REDUCE cannibalism.

posts.post_content: Beak trimming is used as a management strategy for cannibalism because it:

_aimcq_options.text: Reduces the physical capacity to injure other birds
Eliminates the need for adequate space

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Beak trimming reduces the physical capacity of birds to injure each other, serving as a practical management control even when the underlying trigger (crowding, light, nutrition) isn't fully corrected.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Cures the underlying nutritional deficiency: Beak trimming is a physical/mechanical intervention, not a nutritional correction.
  • C. Eliminates the need for adequate space: Incorrect — beak trimming doesn't replace the need to address overcrowding, a separate predisposing factor.
  • D. Increases feather growth rate: Not the mechanism or purpose of beak trimming; it addresses injury capacity, not feather growth.

posts.post_content: Once cannibalism begins in a flock, its rapid spread is mainly driven by:

_aimcq_options.text: The sight of blood attracting other birds to peck the wound
Genetic mutation spreading through the flock

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Once started, cannibalism spreads rapidly because the sight of blood attracts other birds to peck at the wound, escalating injury and mortality if not promptly controlled.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Airborne viral transmission: Cannibalism is a behavioural vice, not an infectious viral process.
  • C. Genetic mutation spreading through the flock: Not the mechanism of cannibalism spread, which is behavioural (visual/blood-triggered), not genetic.
  • D. Increased humidity alone: Not the described mechanism driving the rapid spread of cannibalism within a flock.

posts.post_content: Feather picking is best understood as:

_aimcq_options.text: A milder behavioural vice that can escalate into cannibalism if unresolved
A distinct viral disease unrelated to cannibalism
Always caused by external parasites only
A condition exclusive to male birds

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Feather picking is a milder behavioural vice that can escalate into cannibalism if the underlying triggers (crowding, boredom, nutritional deficiency) are not addressed.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. A distinct viral disease unrelated to cannibalism: Incorrect — feather picking is a behavioural vice, not an infectious viral disease, and is closely linked to cannibalism risk.
  • C. Always caused by external parasites only: Overstates a single cause — while external parasites/irritation can be a factor, feather picking has multiple behavioural/nutritional/environmental causes.
  • D. A condition exclusive to male birds: Incorrect — feather picking is not sex-restricted; it can occur in flocks regardless of sex.

posts.post_content: Self-mutilation in poultry is most closely linked to:

_aimcq_options.text: Boredom and lack of environmental enrichment in confined housing

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Self-mutilation is most closely linked to boredom and lack of environmental enrichment in confined housing, similar to the behavioural drivers of feather picking and cannibalism.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. High dietary vitamin E: Not a described risk factor for self-mutilation; nutritional deficiencies (not vitamin E excess) are the relevant dietary concern for these vices.
  • C. Excess perch space: A protective/preventive factor rather than a contributing cause of self-mutilation.
  • D. Low ambient temperature alone: Not the primary described factor; behavioural/environmental enrichment factors (boredom, crowding) are emphasised instead.

posts.post_content: Provision of environmental enrichment (e.g. perches, pecking objects) helps prevent feather picking primarily by:

_aimcq_options.text: Redirecting pecking behaviour away from flock-mates
Eliminating the need for balanced nutrition

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Environmental enrichment helps by redirecting pecking behaviour away from flock-mates toward appropriate objects, reducing boredom-driven feather picking.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Curing underlying viral infections: Feather picking is a behavioural vice, not a viral infection, so enrichment does not act via curing infection.
  • C. Eliminating the need for balanced nutrition: Incorrect — enrichment addresses behavioural boredom, but adequate nutrition (e.g. sodium, protein) remains a separate necessary preventive measure.
  • D. Increasing stocking density safely: Incorrect — enrichment doesn't make high stocking density "safe"; overcrowding remains a separate risk factor to manage.
